analysis.one_liner: Charges the largest fossil fuel companies $1 trillion for past emissions to fund climate resilience.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 2025 with 25 Democratic cosponsors, was sent to three House committees and has had no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would impose a one-time $1 trillion assessment on fossil fuel extraction and refining companies, with each company's share set by how much of the carbon dioxide released from 2000 through 2023 came from its operations and products. Only companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of emissions would pay, and no company could deduct the payment from its taxes. The money would go into a dedicated fund for disaster recovery, climate resilience projects, and community adaptation, with 40 percent reserved for communities hit hardest by pollution and climate impacts.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and communities facing climate-driven floods, hurricanes, wildfires, and extreme heat, who would get funded disaster response and resilience projects; environmental justice communities, which would receive at least 40 percent of fund spending; and FEMA and local governments, which would get at least $15 billion a year for disaster programs and $6 billion a year for community air and climate grants.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a dedicated fund financed by fossil fuel companies for disaster recovery, climate-resilient infrastructure, wildfire management, public health protections against extreme heat, and water infrastructure upgrades.

Each year, at least $15 billion must go to FEMA for climate disaster response and resilience (including at least $3 billion for pre-disaster community resilience grants) and at least $6 billion for grants under section 138 of the Clean Air Act.

At least 40 percent of fund spending each year must benefit environmental justice communities — communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities that face higher pollution and climate harms.
Companies could pay their share in nine annual installments (20 percent first, then 10 percent each), easing the immediate cash burden while keeping the full obligation in place.

analysis.who_pays: The largest fossil fuel extraction and refining companies — those responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between 2000 and 2023 — would owe a combined $1 trillion, split in proportion to their emissions. Because companies often pass costs to customers, part of the bill could also reach consumers through fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: The biggest oil, gas, and coal companies

drawbacks.text: The assessment is a one-time charge on emissions from 2000 through 2023, not a fee on future pollution, so it would not by itself reduce future emissions or create an ongoing incentive to cut them.
Because fossil fuel companies may pass costs to customers, part of the $1 trillion could show up in gasoline and heating prices rather than coming only out of company profits.
Fund spending is available only as provided in annual appropriations acts, so Congress could leave the money unspent even after companies have paid.
A retroactive tax on emissions from past, legal operations would face strong legal and fairness objections from the companies being charged, an obstacle an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside for ordinary people is large: a trillion dollars of disaster recovery and resilience funding, aimed heavily at the communities most exposed to climate harm. The main costs are that some of the charge could be passed to consumers through energy prices, that it does nothing to cut future emissions, and that it would almost certainly be contested in court as a retroactive tax. On balance, the bill is a serious attempt to shift climate adaptation costs from taxpayers to the companies whose products caused the emissions, though its design leaves room for legal challenge and slow spending.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote since February 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the Polluters Pay Climate Fund Act of 2025 in the House on February 7, 2025.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce committees, with no committee later given clear lead jurisdiction.
The bill has 25 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded.
The complete action history shows no hearing, markup, floor vote, or any other action after the initial referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest fossil fuel companies are better off so far: the $1 trillion assessment never advanced, and the public continues to bear the cost of climate disasters through ordinary taxes and disaster spending.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 25 Democratic cosponsors for a $1 trillion assessment on major fossil fuel emitters.

for.name: 25 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a modest base of support concentrated on one side of the aisle.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill, which was referred to his committee first and sits there without action.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: House majority, controls the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote at any point in the session.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors are Democrats, the sponsor is a Democrat, and no Republican support or action appears anywhere in the record in a Republican-controlled House.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2000 through 2023 would owe a pro-rata share of a $1 trillion assessment, with no tax deduction allowed and joint liability across corporate groups. Their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against the public interest in funded disaster recovery and resilience.

Coal producers above the 1-billion-metric-ton threshold would be assessed based on tonnage extracted (942.5 metric tons of CO2 per million pounds of coal). Like oil and gas, their stake is in preventing the assessment.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action more than a year after introduction, and the bill split across three committees, the realistic path is that it dies quietly at the end of this Congress without a hearing or vote, the usual fate for first-session bills that leadership never schedules.
